messages.subject: Optimization question
parts:
Hello,

I have this problem:

You have 7 types of testers with different test times (in seconds):
T1 T2 T3 T4 T5 T6 T7
98 41 204 177 375 130 281

Each products needs to run through all the testers. The products arrive at a conveyor. The transfer time from conveyor to tester is on average 7.6s (robot). The average movement time from tester to tester is 5s.
You can group testers together in bunches of 24. Any combination of T1-T7 testers in the group is possible. The conveyor connects the different groups of testers. The transfer time between tester groups is 20s. The order in which the tests are run is important.

How many tester of each tester type would you need to optimize throughput? What should be the grouping of the testers? 

And I am trying to solve it by using simmer. I defined a trajectory for the product (3 testers in this case):

env<-simmer("Optimizing throughput")
env

product<-trajectory("sample") %>%
    timeout(function() rnorm(1,0.12)) %>%
    seize("T1",1)%>%
    timeout(function() rnorm(1,1.63)) %>%
    release("T1",1)%>%

    seize("T2",1)%>%
    timeout(function() rnorm(1,0.68)) %>%
    release("T2",1)%>%

    seize("T3",1)%>%
    timeout(function() rnorm(1,3.4)) %>%
    release("T3",1)

envs<-lapply(1:100, function(i){
    simmer() %>%
        add_generator("product", product, at(seq(0,60*4,0.08))) %>%
        add_resource("T1",1) %>%
        add_resource("T2",1) %>%
        add_resource("T3",1) %>%
        run()
})

With one tester of each type, I get 3001 products served in this process with this calculation:

get_mon_arrivals(envs) %>%
    group_by(replication) %>%
    summarise(n=n()) %>%
    .$n %>% mean

And I tried to optimize by using this code:

expand.grid(nr_T1 = 1:10,
            nr_T2 = 1:10,
            nr_T3 = 1:10) %>% nrow()

library(simmer.optim)

sim_model<-function(){
    product<-trajectory("sample") %>%
        timeout(function() rnorm(1,0.12)) %>%
        seize("T1",1)%>%
        timeout(function() rnorm(1,1.63)) %>%
        release("T1",1)%>%
    
        seize("T2",1)%>%
        timeout(function() rnorm(1,0.68)) %>%
        release("T2",1)%>%
    
        seize("T3",1)%>%
        timeout(function() rnorm(1,3.4)) %>%
        release("T3",1)

    env<-simmer() %>%
        add_generator("product", product, at(seq(0,60*4,0.08))) %>%
        add_resource("T1", .opt("nr_T1")) %>%
        add_resource("T2", .opt("nr_T2")) %>%
        add_resource("T3", .opt("nr_T3"))
    
    env
}

set.seed(2016)
r <- simmer_optim(
    model = sim_model,
    method = grid_optim,
    direction = "max",
    objective = msr_arrivals_finished,
    constraints = list(with_args(assert_waiting_time_max, max_val=50000)),
    params = list(nr_T1 = par_discrete(1:10),
                  nr_T2 = par_discrete(1:10),
                  nr_T3 = par_discrete(1:10)
    ),
    control = optim_control(run_args = list(until=8*60)))
r

I really don't have other constraints since the testers will run 24/7 so I only added waiting time to be less than a value. And this is my output:

simmer.optim result 

method:                 grid_optim 
objective value:        1417 
constraints satisfied:  TRUE 

params: 
>  nr_T1 :  9 
>  nr_T2 :  3 
>  nr_T3 :  10 

As I understand, I have produced 1417 products, if I increase the number of testers by the quantities given by the optimization function. Is this correct? If I change my trajectory to include these quantities by tester I still get the same 3001 products I originally calculated... Could you please advise? Any suggestions would be greatly appreciated!

Thanks,

Note that the optimisation has "control = optim_control(run_args =
list(until=8*60))" defined. That simulation time is less than the
original simulation (which was running until all your products, 3001,
were processed), so less products are processed. Use "run(until=8*60)"
in your original simulation and you should get 1400 products
approximately.

Another comment: a normal distribution may not be the best service
time, because it could lead to negative times, which is not possible.
Consider using an exponential, a truncated normal or any other
strictly positive distribution that fits your data.

Iñaki

Iñaki,

Thank you very much for your response. I added the until parameter as suggested and my results were as expected. I also changed to exponential distribution since it will describe best the arrival time of each product. I hope you don't mind but I had a couple of more questions:

1. I initially set up the option of up to three testers per tester type in the optimization model but I wanted to increase it to four but I got an error message: "Error: 'product2436' at 383.06 in 'Release': std:: bad_alloc". I was wondering if you would know what does this mean and how to fix it. 
2. I would also need that the optimization function would limit the total number of testers to choose the best combination of 24 testers. Is there a way to do it?

Thank you so much!

M.

Probably you are running out of memory.
> 2. I would also need that the optimization function would limit the total number of testers to choose the best combination of 24 testers. Is there a way to do it?

Each tester has an average time, which is a parameter of your model,
with 7 possible values. A grid optimisation will eventually find the
optimal combination, but you have a lot of parameters, so it may not
be an option. You can try the other two optimisation methods
supported.

Iñaki
